prompt: The query in the editor has one mistake. Fix it so that it answers this question: for each Dublin day from 1 to 7 December 2025 (by event_date), how many sessions started, and how many ga_session_id values were shared by two or more visitors that day? Use the session_start events that carry both a user_pseudo_id and a ga_session_id; a session is one user_pseudo_id with one ga_session_id. Return three columns, in this order: day (the Dublin day as text, in the same form as event_date), sessions and shared_ids. Return one row for each of those days that has sessions; a day with none has no row. Any row order is fine.
hints: Next, check how the sessions column counts a session.
Two visitors can start a session in the same second and share a ga_session_id, so a count of the ID values counts their two sessions as one.
starter_sql:
WITH starts AS (
  -- one row per session_start event with both IDs, 1 to 7 December 2025 (Dublin days)
  SELECT event_date AS day, user_pseudo_id,
    list_filter(event_params, lambda p: p.key = 'ga_session_id')[1].value.int_value AS ga_session_id
  FROM events
  WHERE event_name = 'session_start'
    AND event_date BETWEEN '20251201' AND '20251207'
    AND user_pseudo_id IS NOT NULL
), per_id AS (
  -- one row per day and ga_session_id: how many visitors started a session with it
  SELECT day, ga_session_id, COUNT(DISTINCT user_pseudo_id) AS visitors
  FROM starts
  WHERE ga_session_id IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY day, ga_session_id
)
SELECT day, COUNT(*) AS sessions, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE visitors > 1) AS shared_ids
FROM per_id
GROUP BY day
why_this_works: Each ga_session_id row carries its number of visitors, and adding those up counts every pair of visitor and ID, which is a session.
